title: Functional Interface — Introduction
summary: Discover Single Abstract Method (SAM) contracts, the @FunctionalInterface annotation, and the architectural bridge connecting OOP interfaces to lambda expressions.
learningObjectives: Define a Functional Interface as an interface specifying exactly ONE abstract method (SAM)
Use the @FunctionalInterface annotation to trigger compile-time validation
Explain why default, static, and Object-inherited methods do not count against the single abstract method rule
Implement functional interfaces using standard anonymous classes and preview lambda syntax
expectedOutcomes: You can define valid functional interfaces complying with SAM rules
You understand why functional interfaces serve as the target types for modern Java lambda expressions

activities.title: Everyday Analogy: The Single-Action Emergency Stop Button

realWorldMetaphor.scenario: In a manufacturing plant or subway station, there is a giant red physical button labeled 'EMERGENCY STOP'. It does not have a menu, a dial, or a multi-option keypad. It does exactly ONE thing: halt machinery immediately when pressed. Anyone can wire this button to a conveyor belt, a nuclear turbine, or an elevator.
realWorldMetaphor.mapping: The Emergency Stop button is a `Functional Interface` (a contract with exactly ONE action: `void execute()`). Because it does only one thing, the consumer doesn't need to specify *which* action to invoke—there is only one possible behavior.
realWorldMetaphor.takeaway: A functional interface has a single responsibility: defining one abstract operation, making it the perfect target for concise behaviors.

activities.title: The SAM Rule & The @FunctionalInterface Annotation
activities.content:
### What is a Functional Interface?

A **Functional Interface** (also known as a **Single Abstract Method** or **SAM** interface) is an interface that contains **exactly one abstract method**.

```java
@FunctionalInterface
public interface StringTransformer {
    String transform(String input); // The ONE abstract method!
}
```

### The Rules of the SAM Count
Does an interface with 5 methods qualify as a functional interface? **YES**, as long as only ONE of those methods is abstract!
1. **Abstract Methods**: Must be **exactly 1**.
2. **Default Methods**: Can have **unlimited** default methods (they have bodies, so they do not count).
3. **Static Methods**: Can have **unlimited** static methods.
4. **`java.lang.Object` Methods**: Re-declaring `equals`, `hashCode`, or `toString` does NOT count against the single abstract method total, because all classes implement them anyway!

```java
@FunctionalInterface
public interface CustomPredicate<T> {
    boolean test(T t); // The 1 abstract method
    
    default CustomPredicate<T> and(CustomPredicate<T> other) { ... } // Ignored in SAM count!
    static void logInfo() { ... }                                    // Ignored in SAM count!
    boolean equals(Object obj);                                      // Ignored in SAM count!
}
```

### The Role of `@FunctionalInterface`
`@FunctionalInterface` is an informative annotation. Just like `@Override`, it is not strictly required for an interface to be functional, but using it instructs the compiler to generate an error if someone accidentally adds a second abstract method.

activities.title: Defining & Implementing a SAM Interface
activities.explanation: PriceModifier has exactly 1 abstract method apply(). printDiscounted() is default, so @FunctionalInterface compiles cleanly. It can be implemented with a class or lambda.

Both a traditional class (`StudentDiscount`) and a modern lambda expression can be assigned to `PriceModifier`.

questions.question: What is the requirement for an interface to be considered a Functional Interface?
options: It must contain exactly one abstract method
It must have zero methods
It must have only static methods
It must implement java.io.Serializable
questions.explanation: A functional interface must contain exactly ONE abstract method (Single Abstract Method / SAM rule).

questions.question: What happens if you annotate an interface with `@FunctionalInterface` and declare two abstract methods inside it?
options: The compiler chooses the first method as the functional method
Compilation error: Unexpected @FunctionalInterface annotation; interface is not a functional interface
A runtime warning is logged
The interface is converted to an abstract class
questions.explanation: The `@FunctionalInterface` annotation instructs javac to verify the SAM contract. Having 2 abstract methods triggers a compile-time error.

questions.question: Can a functional interface contain default methods?
options: No, only abstract methods are allowed
Yes, a functional interface can have an unlimited number of default and static methods
Only one default method is allowed
Only if marked synchronized
questions.explanation: Default and static methods have implementations, so they do NOT count toward the Single Abstract Method count.

questions.question: Which famous interface from `java.lang` is a classic functional interface containing `void run();`?
options: java.lang.Cloneable
java.lang.Runnable
java.lang.Comparable
java.lang.Iterable
questions.explanation: `java.lang.Runnable` defines a single abstract method `public abstract void run();` and is a classic functional interface.

questions.question: Does re-declaring `boolean equals(Object obj)` inside an interface count against the SAM rule?
options: Yes, making it impossible to add any other abstract method
No, public methods declared in java.lang.Object do not count toward the SAM total
Only if equals is marked default
Only in Java 11+
questions.explanation: Public methods from `java.lang.Object` (such as `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString`) are already implemented by all objects and do not count toward the abstract method limit.

questions.question: Is the `@FunctionalInterface` annotation strictly mandatory to create a functional interface?
options: Yes, without it the interface cannot be used with lambdas
No, any interface with exactly one abstract method is automatically functional; the annotation provides compile-time safety checks
Only in package java.util.function
Only if the interface is public
questions.explanation: Just like `@Override`, `@FunctionalInterface` is optional. Any interface with exactly 1 abstract method is structurally a functional interface.

questions.question: Which of the following interfaces is NOT a valid functional interface?
options: interface A { void exec(); }
interface B { void exec(); default void aux() {} }
interface C { void f1(); void f2(); }
interface D { void exec(); static void helper() {} }
questions.explanation: Interface C has 2 abstract methods (`f1()` and `f2()`), which violates the Single Abstract Method (SAM) requirement.

questions.question: What is the primary relationship between functional interfaces and lambda expressions in Java?
options: Lambdas can only return primitive integers
Functional interfaces provide the target type for lambda expressions and method references
Lambdas cannot be assigned to interfaces
Functional interfaces convert lambdas to static methods
questions.explanation: In Java, a lambda expression is an inline implementation of a functional interface; the functional interface determines its target type.

questions.question: Can a functional interface extend another interface?
options: No, functional interfaces cannot participate in inheritance
Yes, as long as the resulting combined interface still has exactly ONE abstract method
Only if the parent interface is empty
Only in Java 17
questions.explanation: A functional interface can extend another interface, provided the total number of abstract methods remains exactly one.

questions.question: What is a major advantage of passing functional interfaces as method arguments?
options: It turns Java into an interpreted language
It enables passing behaviors (functions) as data into methods, decoupling business workflows from custom logic
It bypasses garbage collection
It forces all methods to be static
questions.explanation: Functional interfaces enable higher-order functions: passing dynamic behaviors as arguments to generic algorithms (like filtering, mapping, sorting).

interviewQA.question: What is a SAM interface, and why was the concept formalized in Java 8?
interviewQA.answer: A SAM (Single Abstract Method) interface is an interface that declares exactly one abstract method. Java 8 formalized this concept as 'Functional Interfaces' to serve as the target types for lambda expressions and method references, allowing developers to write expressive functional-style code while maintaining 100% backward compatibility with Java's existing type system.

interviewQA.question: Why don't public methods from `java.lang.Object` count toward the SAM limit in a functional interface?
interviewQA.answer: Any concrete class implementing an interface will implicitly inherit implementations of `equals()`, `hashCode()`, and `toString()` from `java.lang.Object`. Therefore, an abstract method in an interface matching an `Object` signature is already guaranteed to be implemented by every class in Java, so it doesn't represent an unimplemented contract requirement.

interviewQA.question: What are the 4 core built-in functional interfaces in `java.util.function`?
interviewQA.answer: 1. `Predicate<T>`: `boolean test(T t)` — takes an argument, returns boolean. 2. `Function<T, R>`: `R apply(T t)` — takes an argument, transforms and returns a result. 3. `Consumer<T>`: `void accept(T t)` — takes an argument, performs a side-effect, returns void. 4. `Supplier<T>`: `T get()` — takes no arguments, returns a value.

interviewQA.question: What happens if someone deletes the `@FunctionalInterface` annotation from an interface that has 1 abstract method?
interviewQA.answer: Nothing breaks immediately. The interface remains a functional interface based on structural semantics (it still has 1 abstract method) and can still be used with lambda expressions. However, removing the annotation removes compile-time protection, so a future developer could add a second abstract method without realizing they are breaking existing lambda call sites.

interviewQA.question: Can an abstract class with a single abstract method be used as the target type for a lambda expression?
interviewQA.answer: No. In Java, lambda expressions can ONLY target functional interfaces, never abstract classes, even if the abstract class has only one abstract method. This deliberate language decision preserves clean distinction between interfaces and class hierarchies.

interviewQA.question: How are lambdas compiled under the hood in Java bytecode compared to anonymous inner classes?
interviewQA.answer: Anonymous inner classes generate a separate `.class` file on disk (e.g. `Main$1.class`) and allocate a new object on every invocation. Lambdas use the `invokedynamic` (indy) bytecode instruction, using `LambdaMetafactory` to generate and link an optimized call site at runtime, minimizing classloader overhead and memory footprint.

activities.title: Self-Evaluation Checklist
checklist: I understand the Single Abstract Method (SAM) rule for functional interfaces.
I know how to use the @FunctionalInterface annotation to enforce compile-time checks.
I understand why default and static methods do not count toward the SAM rule.
I know why java.lang.Object methods do not count against the SAM limit.
I understand how functional interfaces serve as the target types for lambdas.
I can identify classic functional interfaces like Runnable and Comparable.
I know that abstract classes cannot be functional interfaces, regardless of method count.
I understand how functional interfaces enable passing behaviors as method parameters.
I can write a custom functional interface and implement it with a class or lambda.
I understand the difference in bytecode between anonymous inner classes and invokedynamic.

practiceProblems.title: Custom Math Operation SAM
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Create a single abstract method interface:

1. Functional Interface BinaryMathOp:
   - Annotate with `@FunctionalInterface`
   - Method: int calculate(int a, int b);

2. Class AdditionOp (implements BinaryMathOp):
   - Method: @Override public int calculate(int a, int b) returning a + b

Test in Main:
BinaryMathOp op = new AdditionOp();
Print 'Sum: ' + op.calculate(15, 25);.
hints: In BinaryMathOp, declare: int calculate(int a, int b);
practiceProblems.description: Create a functional interface with a single calculate(int a, int b) method.

practiceProblems.title: String Formatter Functional Pipeline
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a functional string transformer from scratch:

1. Functional Interface StringModifier:
   - Method: String modify(String s);
   - Default Method: default void printModified(String s) printing 'Result: ' + modify(s)

2. Implementing Classes:
   - Class BracketModifier: @Override modify(s) returning '[' + s.toUpperCase() + ']'
   - Class ExclamationModifier: @Override modify(s) returning s + '!!!'

Test in Main:
StringModifier m1 = new BracketModifier(); m1.printModified("java-oop");
StringModifier m2 = new ExclamationModifier(); m2.printModified("HELLO");.
hints: StringModifier has 1 abstract method modify(s) and 1 default method printModified(s).
Test both the class implementation and the lambda implementation.
practiceProblems.description: Add a default printModified() helper to a functional interface from scratch.

practiceProblems.title: Filter Numbers with a Functional Predicate
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Filter an array using a functional interface from scratch:

1. Functional Interface NumberCondition:
   - Method: boolean check(int n);

2. Class NumberFilter:
   - Static Method: public static void filterAndPrint(int[] nums, NumberCondition condition):
     Loop through nums; if condition.check(n) is true, print n.

3. Class EvenNumberCondition (implements NumberCondition):
   - Method: @Override public boolean check(int n) returning n % 2 == 0

Test in Main:
int[] data = { 5, 10, 15, 22, 33, 40 };
NumberFilter.filterAndPrint(data, new EvenNumberCondition());.
hints: Pass a lambda (n) -> n % 2 == 0 as the NumberCondition parameter to filterAndPrint.
practiceProblems.description: Pass a number-testing condition into a filterAndPrint() utility method from scratch.

practiceProblems.title: Fix Violating SAM Rule with Two Abstract Methods
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Fix the compiler error on `@FunctionalInterface`:

Bug: Interface Formatter is marked `@FunctionalInterface`, but declares two abstract methods (`format` and `formatWithPrefix`). The compiler rejects this because functional interfaces must have exactly ONE abstract method!

Your Task:
1. Keep `String format(String val);` as the single abstract method.
2. Make `formatWithPrefix(String prefix, String val)` a `default` method returning `prefix + ": " + format(val)`.

Test in Main:
Formatter fmt = new SimpleFormatter();
Print fmt.formatWithPrefix("INFO", "payload");.
hints: In Formatter, make formatWithPrefix default String formatWithPrefix(String prefix, String val) { return prefix + ": " + format(val); }
SimpleFormatter only needs to override format(String val).
practiceProblems.description: A functional interface can only have ONE abstract method. Make the second method default.

hints: In Transformer.andThen, return a lambda (s) -> next.transform(this.transform(s));
practiceProblems.description: Chain two functional operations sequentially using a default andThen() method from scratch.
